body:
Superseded as a standalone decision by **MAPPING_SEMANTICS.md Section 3** (#237, 8bbb0add), which settles this class in one rule:

> One MIM record per distinct substance. A record's `identifier` is the most specific stable id that denotes *that* substance. Never express a more specific thing by sharing a broader term's identifier.

with an ordered decision procedure — exact ontology term → else the substance's own `cas:` → else a minted `kgmicrobe.compound:`, always `narrowMatch` + registry row for the specificity gap.

This issue stays **open for its execution**, which is deliberately not in #237: applying the rule to the 61 duplicate-identifier groups is a curation batch, and both tools have limits that need addressing first — `reground_mapped_record.py` refuses when the destination CURIE is already held (true for the headline cases, which need reground *and* merge together), and every baseline row is `collection=mapped`, so the 15 merges need MAPPED-to-MAPPED tooling that does not exist yet.

Note the dispositions in `mappings/duplicate_identifier_baseline.tsv` are only renamed where a verdict was reached by *reading the records*. A first attempt to derive all 61 by rule got at least three exactly backwards — `CHEBI:32150`, `CHEBI:91248` and `CHEBI:86158` are shared terms that **are** the hydrate, so those groups merge rather than split. The 32 `HYDRATE_FAMILY_UNREVIEWED` rows remain honestly unreviewed.

The mechanical half is done in #252 (69a02f36): `docs/data/label_index.csv` publishes one row per (label, record) with a `match_type`, ordered **MAPPED before non-MAPPED, then preferred_term before synonym**, so resolution is "take the first row and use its `identifier`".

That deterministically settles **16 of the 87**. Review caught that my first ordering resolved 21 labels to *rejected* records — `Bacto Soytone` went to the dead `CHEBI:8150` tombstone rather than the live `FOODON:03315720` — and that `identifier` is not a unique record key, so 188 labels tied completely and were decided by YAML order. Both fixed and tested.

**Keeping this open for the remaining 69**, which no precedence rule can settle: they are synonym-vs-synonym, i.e. two records genuinely answering to one name. Most are the #225 class — one substance under two identifiers — and need a curation decision per group, not a rule. `label_index.csv` is now the worklist for them: group by `label`, keep the ones with more than one distinct `identifier` and no MAPPED `preferred_term` row.

Related: #252, #225, #229, #237.

**Re-measured today: this is now 337, not 87 — roughly 4× the filed number.**

It also matters more than when it was filed. Since #260 merged, CultureMech resolves groundings through `docs/data/label_index.csv`, so an ambiguous label is no longer a presentation wart — the consumer silently takes whichever row sorts first.

Breakdown of the 337:

| shape | count |
|---|---|
| synonym-only collision | 240 |
| preferred_term vs synonym | 96 |
| two preferred_terms | 1 |

**199 resolve across different ontologies**, i.e. they give genuinely different answers rather than two spellings of one:

```
'(2s)-2-aminobutanedioic acid'  ->  CHEBI:17053      L-Aspartic acid
                                    cas:1115-63-5    L-Aspartic acid potassium salt
                                    cas:323194-76-9  L-Aspartic acid sodium salt monohydrate
```

That example shows the root cause, and it is one bug rather than 337: **salt and hydrate records inherit the free acid's systematic name as a synonym.** The parent compound's own name then resolves to the parent plus every salt of it.

So the fix is probably a rule about which records may carry a parent's synonym, not 337 individual adjudications — and that rule would also close chunks of #315, #245, #251 and #225, which are the same over-inheritance seen from other angles.

PR #383 fixes the **ordering** half of this. The remaining work is curation, and it is a different problem — recording the split so the issue does not read as one undifferentiated pile of 337.

## What #383 fixes: 16 labels resolved to the wrong record

Not ambiguity in the sense of "two defensible answers" — these were cases where the index had the right answer available and returned a different one:

| label | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `citric acid` | CHEBI:53258 **Trisodium citrate** | CHEBI:30769 Citric acid |
| `fructose` | cas:308066-66-2 **Fructooligosaccharides** | CHEBI:28757 Fructose |
| `asparagine` | CHEBI:17196 **L**-Asparagine | CHEBI:22653 Asparagine |
| `FeSO4 x 7H2O` | CHEBI:75832 FeSO4 x 5 **H2O** | CHEBI:75836 (heptahydrate) |

Two causes: the raw `label` sorted above every semantic key so an ALL-CAPS synonym beat the owning record (**my regression from #378**), and ownership did not outrank MAPPED-ness so a heptahydrate label got answered with the pentahydrate.

**Labels owned by a record that resolve to that record: 80 → 96 of 96. Owner-exists-but-loses: 16 → 0.**

## What remains: 240 labels no record owns

This is where the real curation question lives, and my earlier comment overstated how much of it the salt-inheritance story explains. Current breakdown of the 336:

| shape | count | status |
|---|---|---|
| a record owns the label | 96 | **resolved by precedence** (#383) |
| no record owns it — synonym/term-label only | 239 | open |
| two records claim it as preferred_term | 1 | open |

The 239 are typically a parent's systematic name carried as a synonym by several of its salts or hydrates, with no record for the parent itself:

```
'(2R)-2,3-dihydroxypropyl dihydrogen phosphate'
    -> cas:17989-41-2   sn-Glycerol 3-phosphate lithium salt
    -> cas:29849-82-9   sn-Glycerol 3-phosphate bis(cyclohexylammonium) salt
```

But not all of them are that shape — a good number are ChEBI modelling distinctions rather than over-inheritance, e.g. `(2R)-2-ammonio-3-sulfanylpropanoate` on both `L-Cysteine` (CHEBI:17561) and `L-cysteine zwitterion` (CHEBI:35235), where both records legitimately carry the name. Those need a different remedy than a synonym-ownership rule.

So the next step is to partition the 239 by cause before proposing a rule, rather than assuming one explains them all. Ordering cannot help here: with no owning record, any first row is a deterministic but arbitrary pick.

`LABEL_INDEX_CONTRACT.md` now states this explicitly so a consumer does not read a first row as unambiguous.

## Partition of the unowned ambiguous labels, by cause

#383 fixed the ordering half: every label a record *owns* now resolves to that record (97 of 97). What remained was 240 labels **no record claims as its `preferred_term`**, where the first row is a deterministic but arbitrary pick. I said these needed partitioning by cause before any rule. Here it is.

### First: a fifth of them were not chemistry at all

The highest-multiplicity "labels" in the whole index were curation annotations:

```
'properties: defined component, organic compound, simple component'   19 identifiers
'properties: defined component, simple component, organic compound'   15
'role: carbon source'                                                 14
```

`_NOT_A_LABEL` in `export_lists.py` was meant to exclude these but required **both** keywords in one string (`^\s*Role:.*;\s*Properties:`). The importer also writes them split, so `Role: Carbon source` and `Properties: …` each passed through as a resolvable label. **183 rows, 80 labels.**

Fixed on `analysis/232-partition-unowned-labels`: **337 → 316 ambiguous, 240 → 219 unowned**, and all 232 filtered strings verified to be annotations rather than names.

### The remaining 219, partitioned by whether the competitors are the same substance

String similarity was too weak to partition on — it called `sn-Glycerol 3-phosphate lithium salt` vs `bis(cyclohexylammonium) salt` "different cores". Using the records' own `molecular_formula` instead:

| group | count | what it means | remedy |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **different formulas** | **167** | genuinely different substances share one label | the real harm — see below |
| one formula known, rest blank | 32 | undecidable; needs chemistry backfill | #316-adjacent |
| same formula | 12 | one substance, notation differs | harmless; any first row is right |
| no formula anywhere | 8 | undecidable (mixtures, mints, ENVO) | manual |

### The 167 are the salt-inheritance pattern, now measured rather than asserted

```
'(2s)-2-aminobutanedioic acid'                 <- L-aspartic acid's systematic name
    CHEBI:17053      C4H7NO4     L-Aspartic acid
    cas:1115-63-5    C4H6KNO4    L-Aspartic acid potassium salt
    cas:323194-76-9  C4H8NNaO5   L-Aspartic acid sodium salt monohydrate
```

The free acid's systematic name is carried as a synonym by its salts, so a consumer asking for the acid can be handed a salt. The formulas differ — potassium, sodium, an extra water — so this is not a notation quibble.

**But my earlier claim that this was one root cause explaining the whole set was wrong.** It explains this group. It does not explain the 12 same-formula cases, which are ChEBI modelling distinctions rather than over-inheritance:

```
'(2r)-2-ammonio-3-sulfanylpropanoate'
    CHEBI:17561  C3H7NO2S  L-Cysteine
    CHEBI:35235  C3H7NO2S  L-cysteine zwitterion
```

Both records legitimately carry that name; ChEBI models the neutral species and the zwitterion separately. Nothing is wrong and no synonym should be removed — picking either is correct.

### Proposed remedy for the 167, for comment before I build it

Pruning 167 synonyms by hand assumes we know which record each name *should* denote, and for an unowned label nothing in the corpus states that. Two options that do not require that knowledge:

1. **Publish the ambiguity.** Add an `ambiguous` column (or emit no row) when competing identifiers disagree on formula. `LABEL_INDEX_CONTRACT` currently promises *take the first row*, and for these that promise hands over an arbitrary pick among genuinely different substances. Saying "this label does not identify one substance" is honest and machine-readable.
2. **Prune at the source**, by rule: a record whose formula differs from a competitor's must not carry a synonym that the competitor also carries. Automatable, but it deletes curated data on a heuristic, and gets the direction wrong wherever the *salt* is the thing a recipe actually means.

I lean to (1) — it is reversible, loses no curation, and turns a silent wrong answer into a visible unknown. (2) can then be applied case by case where a curator confirms the direction.

Not proceeding with either until there is a view on it, since (2) is destructive and (1) changes a published contract.

Re-measured on `origin/main` (`docs/data/label_index.csv`), because my last sweep ranked this issue without checking it — I had measured SSSOM subject/label pairs, which is a different surface, and said so rather than let the 0 stand.

**It has grown since filing:**

| | filed | now |
|---|---:|---:|
| labels resolving to more than one identifier | 87 | **114** |
| preferred_term-vs-synonym collisions | 18 | **37** |

By the index's own `ambiguity` verdict, on the colliding labels:

```
conflict:different_substances    48
resolved:owned                   37
unresolved:partial_chemistry     22
agree:same_substance              5
unresolved:no_chemistry           2
```

The **48 `conflict:different_substances`** are the subset that matters: the index has already judged those labels to name genuinely different substances, so a consumer resolving by name gets a wrong answer rather than an ambiguous one. `agree:same_substance` (5) is harmless, and `resolved:owned` (37) is the owner logic working as designed.

Examples of the CAS-vs-CHEBI shape that dominates:

```
'(2s)-2-aminobutanedioic acid'   CHEBI:17053, cas:1115-63-5, cas:323194-76-9
'(2r)-2-ammonio-3-sulfanylpropanoate'  CHEBI:17561, CHEBI:35235
'(2r)-2,3-dihydroxypropyl dihydrogen phosphate'  cas:17989-41-2, cas:29849-82-9
```

Two CAS numbers under one systematic name is usually a stereochemistry or hydrate distinction the label does not carry — the same family as #454/#455/#456.

Related work since: #669 pins the equivalent defect in the SSSOM `other` column (Rule K, 115 tokens across 106 rows baselined), and Rule H already pins it for `subject_label`. Neither covers the label index, which is what this issue is about.

No change proposed here — this is a measurement update so the issue's numbers reflect the current corpus, and so the 48-row conflict subset is visible as the actionable core rather than the full 114.

Progress on the 47-label `conflict:different_substances` core (re-measured after #699: 111 colliding labels, 47 conflicts). **7 of 47 triaged, all RETIRE_SYNONYM** — every one the same shape: a salt or hydrate record carrying the parent acid's IUPAC name as an EXACT_SYNONYM (e.g. `(2S)-2-aminopentanedioic acid` on the monopotassium glutamate monohydrate record; `3-hydroxybutanoic acid` on poly-3-hydroxybutyrate). The one that was adversarially verified before the run hit its session limit survived (glutamate). 40 remain untriaged and the 7 proposals are unapplied; the mechanism for applying them already exists (`scripts/retire_wrong_compound_synonyms.py`, #699).

**Applied in #732**: 57 synonyms on 23 records retired (`REJECTED_LABEL`) — the 40 triaged label conflicts collapsed to one shape (a form carrying its parent's or a sibling hydrate's name), verified mechanically against ChEBI names and water counts since the skeptic stage never ran. Label index after regeneration: colliding labels **111 → 75**, `conflict:different_substances` **47 → 11**. The 11 that remain either involve names ChEBI does not carry (left for a curator) or were the 6 items the run never reached.

**Landed in #732 (`c5993f67`)** — and not the way first proposed. The review lock from #729–#731 pins every reviewed record's YAML hash, so the 57 retirements were re-expressed as a *bounded synonym-only refresh* in `reports/sssom_completion_20260921/parent_names/`, mirroring how #703 was landed: a frozen `decisions.json`, an `apply.py` that writes through the validated path, a refresh vetoed by the pinned claw producer, and the assembler chained across both refreshes. Dispositions unchanged (1,763 / 1,255); nothing approved was withdrawn.

Label index after: colliding labels **111 → 75**, `conflict:different_substances` **47 → 11**.

What remains here:
- the **11** residual conflicts: names ChEBI does not carry (`a-Ketoglutaric acid`, `Na2-citrate` — #704) plus the 6 items the triage run never reached;
- **#733**: 11 retired names whose rightful owner record never listed them — a *move*, not a mint;
- the 37 preferred-term-vs-synonym collisions that are stereo-vs-generic pairs (`ASPARTIC ACID` ↔ L-aspartic acid) belong to #454's family, not here.

Any further synonym change on a reviewed record must go through the same bundle mechanism; the two review checks (`reviewed-sssom`, `supported-graph`) now enforce that on every PR.

**Residual conflicts cleared (#757, main `0b4d0f0f`).** After #732 and the four #312 batches, 29 label-index rows were still `conflict:different_substances`. Every one was a synonym naming a different chemical form than its record (an anhydrous term's ChEBI names on CoCl2 x 2/x 4/x 6 H2O, NaH2PO4 x 2 H2O and Na2MoO4·2H2O; trisodium citrate's systematic name on two sodium citrate dihydrate tombstones; the dihydrate labels on the anhydrous Calcium Chloride tombstone; the free acid's name on the disodium alpha-ketoglutarate hydrate; the anion's name on the Na-glutamate tombstone) or not a name at all (`Optional ingredient`, a CultureMech annotation on four compounds). 18 tokens on 14 records are now `REJECTED_LABEL`, each checked against `chebi.db` and the owning record at apply time. **`conflict:different_substances`: 29 → 0.**

Not touched: the citrate salt identities themselves (#704) and the 37 stereo-vs-generic preferred-term collisions (#454's family). #733 closed (no recipe names any of the 11 gaps). One related defect surfaced and is deferred behind #740: the dihydrate record still carries three NaH2PO4 monohydrate spellings whose 40 recipes count under anhydrous NaH2PO4 (#758); the fix is in the repo and verified, waiting on the identity-plan pin.
